body_markdown:
The Ford Thunderbird went through 11 generations during its half-century production run. At the[beginning](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/1955-57-ford-thunderbird-buyers-guide/) and[end](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/fords-2002-05-thunderbird-could-finally-fly-as-a-future-classic/) of that period, it arrived in showrooms as a sporty two-seat convertible, while in between those bookends it manifested as everything from[a four-door sedan](https://oldcarbrochures.org/United%20States/Ford_Thunderbird/1971-Ford-Thunderbird/1971-Ford-Thunderbird-Brochure/slides/1971_Ford_Thunderbird-08-09.html) to[a two-and-a-half-ton behemoth of a coupe](https://oldcarbrochures.org/United%20States/Ford_Thunderbird/1975_Ford_Thunderbird/1975_Thunderbird_Brochure/index.html) . Today’s Final Parking Space is an example of the only T-Bird that could hold its own against its European rivals on a road course, found at[the Pick-n-Pull](https://www.picknpull.com/locations/175/salinas-ca) in[John Steinbeck’s California hometown](https://www.seemonterey.com/blog/john-steinbeck-salinas/) .


Ford Motor Company


The[Thunderbird Turbo Coupe](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/thunderbird-turbo-coupe-is-a-treasure/) was built for the 1983 through 1988 model years, and the 1987-1988 models with manual transmissions[are the best performers of that ninth generation](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/fords-thunderbird-turbo-coupe-is-soaring-once-again/) .


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


That’s what we’ve got for today’s FPS subject: a genuine late Fox Thunderbird with three pedals, 15 pounds of intercooled boost courtesy of an IHI turbocharger, and just about every expensive option available *other* than the power-draining automatic transmission.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


This is the second Thunderbird we’ve had in this series, after[a massive 1969 Two-Door Landau with a 360-horse brute of a 429 engine](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/final-parking-space/final-parking-space-1969-ford-thunderbird-two-door-landau/) in a San Francisco Bay Area boneyard last year.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


In recent years,[most of the Thunderbirds](https://www.row52.com/Search?Page=1&MakeId=132&ModelId=1914&Year=&SortDirection=asc&Distance=50&ZipCode=&Sort=Year&HasImage=&HasComment=&LocationId=0&V1=&V2=&V3=&V4=&V5=&V6=&V7=&V8=&V9=&V10=&V11=&V12=&V13=&V14=&V15=&V16=&V17=&YMMorVIN=YMM&IsVin=false) you’ll find in self-service junkyards will be of the 1989-1997 tenth-generation MN12 variety, with[a sprinkling of cars](https://www.murileemartin.com/Junkyard/JunkyardGallery-Ford.html) from the early 1960s through the Fox-body era. I have yet to photograph a 2002-2005 T-Bird in a car graveyard, but it’s bound to happen eventually.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


Before you get your hopes up about rescuing this car from the crusher, be aware that it’s *very* rusty. California cars tend to corrode very little… unless they live within a few blocks of the Pacific, where salt kicked up by crashing waves finds its way into the fog every morning and settles on parked cars. They rust from the top down, the opposite of their counterparts in the Midwest, and I’ve[seen](https://www.autoblog.com/news/junkyard-gem-1964-pontiac-catalina-custom-ventura) some[horrifically](http://www.thetruthaboutcars.com/2015/06/junkyard-find-1974-cadillac-fleetwood-terrifying-ocean-rust-edition/) rusty[cars](http://www.thetruthaboutcars.com/2013/10/junkyard-find-1984-toyota-van-with-bonus-san-francisco-beachfront-rust/) in junkyards near the California coast.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


That’s what we’ve got here. This car sat outside near the ocean for many years, gradually building up a coat of lichens and moss as diluted brine trickled down its flanks.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


This Ford supported a whole ecosystem of[lichens and the creatures that live among them](https://sbbotanicgarden.org/insight/rare-lichens-in-california/) , probably for decades.


California Bureau of Automotive Repair


Plugging its VIN into[the California Smog Check History site](https://www.bar.ca.gov/inspection) shows that its most recent emissions test was more than 20 years ago.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


The build tag tells us that this car was assembled at Lorain Assembly in Ohio. The paint is Oxford White and the interior is done up in Raven cloth and vinyl.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


The engine is the 2.3-liter SOHC straight-four best-known for its use in[the Pinto](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/final-parking-space/final-parking-space-1978-ford-pinto-3-door-runabout/) , but with *much* more power thanks to what amounted to the same intercooled turbocharging rig that went into[the previous year’s Mustang SVO](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/turns-out-the-mustang-svo-won-after-all/comment-page-2/) .


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


This lightweight engine made 190 horsepower and 240 pound-feet, serious stuff for a 3380-pound car in 1987. If you got the automatic transmission behind this engine, though, you gave up 40 horses and 40 pound-feet.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


With its MSRP of $16,805 (about $51,006 in 2026 dollars), this car had more power than and weighed exactly the same as a new BMW 633CSi, which listed at $46,965 ($142,547 after inflation). Sure, the pricey Bavarian coupe had an independent rear suspension and more snob appeal, but a Turbo Coupe with a good driver could walk away from it on a race track.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


In 1987, American Ford shoppers could pay a mere $11,835 ($35,921 in today’s money) for a new Mustang GT hatchback with 225 horsepower and 300 pound-feet from its[5.0-liter Windsor V-8](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gMbxOUgPDsI) , but that car was unsophisticated and cramped next to its Turbo Coupe big brother.


Merkur


But what about a new[Merkur XR4Ti](https://www.hagerty.com/media/entertainment/merkur-xr4ti-the-american-sierra-and-fords-perfect-mistake/) for $17,832 ($53,123 now)? This was no Detroit car trying to beat European coupes at their own game; this was a genuine German-built machine with a slightly less powerful version of the Turbo Coupe’s engine.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


Because this car had no knock sensor, the driver had to know to select the fuel type before standing on the throttle.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


This car was built with the Electronic Equipment Group, a $365 option package ($1108 after inflation) that included the keyless-entry feature.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


The power moonroof was standard equipment on the 1987 Turbo Coupe.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


It didn’t quite reach 140,000 miles during its career.


Ford


The following generation of Thunderbird was built on[the larger MN12 platform](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/a-v-8-couldnt-save-fords-directionless-mn12-platform/) , shared with the[Lincoln Mark VIII](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/1995-mark-viii-strong-finish-to-the-era-of-lincoln-coupes/) . There was a[Super Coupe](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/1989-95-thunderbird-sc-misunderstood-muscle/) version, equipped with a supercharged Essex V-6 that made a bit more horsepower and a *lot* more torque than the turbo 2.3 engine in its predecessor. Unlike the Fox Thunderbird, this car had an independent rear suspension. Sales weren’t what Dearborn had hoped for, but that was caused more by the American cultural shift to trucks than by any fault of the tenth-gen T-Bird.


Now with *computers* .


Jackie Stewart liked it.


Shouldn’t the guy next to the car be riding a[mythical bird](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thunderbird_(mythology)) instead of a horse?
